findings.who: A Yonkers resident, or a self-employed filer in the MCTA region who pays the metropolitan commuter transportation mobility tax (MCTMT) by estimated payments. They want part of the overpayment to cover 2026 Yonkers surcharge or MCTMT estimates.
findings.why_no: "Your 2026 New York tax" may read as New York State income tax only. The filer may enter zero, or a smaller amount, thinking the Yonkers or MCTMT estimate cannot be paid from the refund.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 23, Line 79: "Enter the amount of overpayment from line 77 that you want applied to your New York State, New York City, Yonkers, and metropolitan commuter transportation mobility tax estimated tax for 2026."
findings.fix: Ask: "How much of your New York overpayment should be applied to your 2026 estimated tax (New York State, New York City, Yonkers and MCTMT)?"

findings.who: A filer who directs part of the overpayment to NYS 529 accounts on Form IT-195 (line 78a).
findings.why_no: The help says "The rest is refunded to you." The filer may lower or misjudge the line 79 amount, thinking the remainder all comes back as a refund. The instructions say lines 78a through 79 together should equal line 77.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 23, Line 79: "The total of lines 78a through 79 should equal the amount on line 77."
findings.fix: Help: "The rest goes to any NYS 529 deposits you choose and is otherwise refunded to you."

findings.who: Spouses filing jointly who plan to make 2026 estimated payments, or where only the spouse expects 2026 self-employment or MCTMT liability.
findings.why_no: "Your 2026 New York tax" may read as the asking spouse's own tax only, so the couple may apply less than they intend.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 23, Line 79: "Enter the amount of overpayment from line 77 that you want applied to your ... estimated tax for 2026."
findings.fix: On joint returns, say "your and your spouse's 2026 estimated tax".

used.revision: Form IT-201-I (2025), Instructions for Form IT-201 (including instructions for Forms IT-195 and IT-201-ATT), 41 pages; final 2025 edition; PDF modified 2025-11-20
locators: p. 23, Line 79: Estimated tax, "Enter the amount of overpayment from line 77 that you want applied to your New York State, New York City, Yonkers, and metropolitan commuter transportation mobility tax estimated tax for 2026."

findings.who: A commuter domiciled in Connecticut, New Jersey or Westchester who keeps a Manhattan apartment all year and spends 184 or more days (counting part days) in New York City.
findings.why_no: "Did you live in New York City ... for all of 2025?" asks where the filer lived. The help covers only time away from a city home. This filer's home is in the suburbs, so the truthful answer is no.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 30: "You maintain a permanent place of abode in New York State for substantially all of the tax year and spend 184 days or more in New York State"; p. 31: "substitute New York City or Yonkers in place of New York State"
findings.fix: Ask about the statutory test directly. First ask whether the filer (or spouse) kept a place to live in New York City for nearly all of 2025. If yes, ask how many days, counting any part of a day, they spent in the city. Treat a city resident as anyone domiciled in the city or meeting both parts of the test, then route on that result.

findings.who: A filer domiciled in New York City who spent all of 2025 on a temporary work assignment in Atlanta or abroad. They sublet or gave up the city apartment, plan to return, and visited the city more than 30 days, so the Group A exception does not apply.
findings.why_no: The help counts time away only "if your home stayed in the city". With no city apartment, the filer did not "live" in the city at all in 2025 and answers no. Their domicile is still the city.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 30: "If you move to a new location but intend to stay there only for a limited amount of time (no matter how long), your domicile does not change." Also: "Your domicile is New York State. However ... you are not a resident if you meet all three of the conditions in either Group A or Group B"
findings.fix: Ask separately whether the filer's permanent home, the place they intend to return to, was in New York City all year, even if they lived elsewhere temporarily. Apply the Group A and Group B exceptions only after a yes.

findings.who: A filer who moved from Brooklyn to Florida in 2025 but kept the Brooklyn apartment, kept their job ties and family in the city, and expects to come back. The move does not meet the clear-and-convincing standard for a change of domicile.
findings.why_no: The filer reads "for all of 2025" by the calendar: they moved out in the spring, so they answer no.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 30: "A change of domicile is clear and convincing only when your primary ties are clearly greater in the new location." Also: "Your New York domicile does not change until you can demonstrate that you have abandoned your New York domicile"
findings.fix: After a no, ask whether the filer moved away from the city in 2025. If so, ask whether they kept their city home and their main ties there. If they did, treat them as still domiciled in the city, or refer them for a domicile review.

findings.who: A graduate, law or medical student, or a full-time undergraduate's spouse, who is domiciled elsewhere and lives all year in university housing in Manhattan, spending more than 184 days in the city.
findings.why_no: The help says "A college dorm does not count as a home." The student reads it as covering every student residence and answers no. The exclusion applies only to full-time undergraduates in a baccalaureate program.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 30: "a residence maintained by a full-time student enrolled at an institution of higher education in an undergraduate degree program leading to a baccalaureate degree and occupied by the student while attending the institution is not a permanent place of abode with respect to that student"
findings.fix: Change the help to: "Housing you occupied as a full-time undergraduate student working toward a bachelor's degree does not count as a place to live. Graduate students' university housing does count."

findings.who: A commuter who keeps a city apartment and counts only nights slept there (for example 150). Counting every workday they set foot in the city, they reach more than 184 days.
findings.why_no: Neither the gate help nor the State question help says that any part of a day counts as a day. The filer counts nights and decides they did not live in the city.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 30: "*Any part of a day is a day for this purpose."
findings.fix: Ask for a day count with this help: "Count every day you were in New York City for any part of the day, including commuting days."

findings.who: A joint filer who moved into the city mid-2025 while their spouse lived in the city all year, or who lived in the city all year while the spouse lived elsewhere.
findings.why_no: The gate says "you", while the line's helper tests "you (and your spouse, on a joint return)". Spouses with different residency statuses may need different handling for the joint return, and the gate question does not ask about the spouse.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 30: "A permanent place of abode usually includes a residence your spouse owns or leases." Also, Group B: "You, your spouse (unless legally separated) and minor children spent 90 days or less"
findings.fix: Ask the gate as "Did you and your spouse each ...", record each spouse's answer, and route mixed answers to the part-year or nonresident path.

findings.who: A member of the military, or a military spouse, whose legal residence is New York City but who is stationed or living elsewhere.
findings.why_no: The filer has not lived in the city for the year and answers no. Their residency is governed by special SCRA rules that the gate does not mention.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 30: "Note: Special rules under the SCRA apply to members of the military and their spouses for determining residency."
findings.fix: Add a screening question: "Were you or your spouse in active military service, or a military spouse, in 2025?" Route a yes to the military residency rules.

used.revision: Form IT-201-I (2025), Instructions for Form IT-201 (including instructions for Forms IT-195 and IT-201-ATT), 41 pages; final 2025 edition; PDF modified 2025-11-20
locators: p. 30, Resident, "You maintain a permanent place of abode in New York State for substantially all of the tax year and spend 184 days or more in New York State during the tax year"
p. 31, New York City and Yonkers, "substitute New York City or Yonkers in place of New York State"

findings.who: A New York resident is the beneficiary of a trust or estate. The fiduciary made 2025 estimated payments and allocated part of them to the beneficiary on its notice. The beneficiary and their spouse made no payments of their own.
findings.why_no: The gate asks whether 'you (or ... your spouse)' paid New York income tax ahead of time. The fiduciary paid, not the filer. Its help lists only the filer's own estimated payments, a 2024 refund and an extension payment. The trust-allocation help appears only with the gated amount question, which is never reached after a no.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 22: 'If you are a beneficiary of an estate or trust and are claiming your portion of any payment of estimated taxes allocated to you by the estate or trust, include your amount on line 75'
findings.fix: Add to the gate: '... or did an estate or trust you are a beneficiary of allocate estimated tax payments to you?' Repeat in the gate's help: 'Include estimated tax an estate or trust allocated to you on its notice to you.'

findings.who: A self-employed filer in the MCTD region (for example, a consultant in Westchester or New York City) made 2025 estimated payments only for the metropolitan commuter transportation mobility tax. A spouse's wage withholding covered their income tax.
findings.why_no: The gate asks only about 'New York income tax.' The MCTMT is a tax on net earnings from self-employment, not an income tax. A filer who paid only MCTMT estimates truthfully answers no.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 22, Line 75: 'your 2025 estimated tax payments for New York State, New York City, Yonkers, and metropolitan commuter transportation mobility tax'
findings.fix: Reword the gate: '... pay New York State, New York City or Yonkers income tax, or the metropolitan commuter transportation mobility tax (MCTMT), for 2025 ahead of time ...'

findings.who: A New York City or Yonkers resident made 2025 estimated payments that they think of as city tax, for example payments sized to cover NYC resident tax on investment income. They do not regard these as payments of state tax.
findings.why_no: The phrase 'New York income tax', with no mention of the city taxes, is easily read as New York State tax only. The gate's help does not say that City and Yonkers payments count. Only the gated question's help says so.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 22, Line 75: 'estimated tax payments for New York State, New York City, Yonkers, and metropolitan commuter transportation mobility tax'
findings.fix: Name New York City and Yonkers income tax in the gate question itself, as in the MCTMT fix above, and state in the gate help that payments of any of these taxes count.

findings.who: A filer whose only payment was made with Form IT-370 (or IT-370-V online) on the April 15, 2026 due date, with the extension request.
findings.why_no: A payment made on the due date in 2026 may not feel like paying 2025 tax 'ahead of time'. The help does list the extension payment, which mitigates this.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 22: 'any amount you paid with Form IT-370, Application for Automatic Six-Month Extension of Time to File for Individuals (or Form IT-370-V ...)'
findings.fix: Put the extension payment in the question itself: '... or make a payment with an extension request (Form IT-370) ...'

findings.who: A filer had a 2024 overpayment credited to 2025 estimated tax, and the Tax Department later adjusted the credit. Or the filer recalls the 2024 overpayment as a 'credit carried forward', not a refund.
findings.why_no: The word 'refund' may not match how the filer remembers an overpayment that was never paid out to them.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 22: 'any amount of overpayment from your 2024 personal income tax return that you applied to your 2025 estimated tax (if this amount was adjusted by the Tax Department, use the adjusted amount)'
findings.fix: Use 'a 2024 overpayment (refund) credited to your 2025 estimated tax, including an amount the Tax Department adjusted'.

used.revision: Form IT-201-I (2025), Instructions for Form IT-201 (including instructions for Forms IT-195 and IT-201-ATT), 41 pages; final 2025 edition; PDF modified 2025-11-20
locators: p. 22, Line 75: Total estimated tax payments and amount paid with Form IT-370, "your 2025 estimated tax payments for New York State, New York City, Yonkers, and metropolitan commuter transportation mobility tax"

findings.who: A married couple files jointly. The spouse made untaxed online or out-of-state purchases while the couple kept a New York home for only part of 2025. The filer answering bought nothing untaxed.
findings.why_no: The gate asks only 'did you buy anything'. Unlike the gated helper, it does not say 'you (or, on a joint return, your spouse)', so the filer truthfully answers no for themselves.
findings.line: ny_it201.gate.use_tax_abode (and the line 59 amount it prorates)
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 18, Line 59: 'You owe sales or compensating use tax if you: • purchased an item or service subject to tax that is delivered to you in New York State without payment of New York State and local tax to the seller'
findings.fix: Ask: 'In 2025, did you (or, on a joint return, your spouse) buy anything ...'

findings.who: A New York resident buys an item in New Jersey or Pennsylvania, pays that state's sales tax, and brings it home to New York, where the combined rate is higher.
findings.why_no: They paid sales tax on it, and they read 'taxable in New York' as excluding a purchase another state taxed. Only a lower rate than New York City's is mentioned, so a filer outside NYC sees nothing that applies to them.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 18: 'purchased an item or service outside New York State that is subject to tax in New York State ... with subsequent use in New York State.' Note: 'You may be entitled to a credit for sales tax paid to another state.'
findings.fix: Add to the help: 'Count a purchase taxed by another state at a lower rate than your New York rate; you owe the difference.'

findings.who: A resident of a higher-rate New York locality (outside NYC) buys an item in a lower-rate New York county, pays that county's tax, and uses the item at home.
findings.why_no: They did pay New York sales tax. The help names only a rate 'lower than New York City's', so they take the gate as not covering an intra-state rate difference.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 18: 'You may also owe an additional local tax if you use property or services in another locality in New York State ... and its rate of tax is higher than the rate of tax originally paid.'
findings.fix: Change the help to: 'Count a purchase taxed at a lower rate than the rate where you live in New York.'

findings.who: A filer bought cigarettes, fuel or other goods on an Indian reservation, not under Oneida Nation taxes, and paid no New York tax.
findings.why_no: They read the reservation sale as not taxable in New York. The examples ('online, by mail, or in another state') omit reservations.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 18: 'An unpaid sales or use tax liability commonly occurs if you made purchases ... on an Indian reservation (except for purchases subject to Oneida Nation taxes)'
findings.fix: Add 'on an Indian reservation (other than Oneida Nation)' and 'by catalog or TV shopping' to the examples.

findings.who: A filer paid for a taxable service, such as out-of-state repair or storage of property used in New York, without New York tax.
findings.why_no: They read 'buy anything' as goods only, not services.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 18: 'purchased an item or service subject to tax ...'
findings.fix: Say 'buy any item or taxable service'.

findings.who: A filer, or a married couple filing jointly, with significant non-wage income in 2025, such as self-employment, rent, gains or a large bonus with little withholding. They made no New York estimated tax payments at all, so line 75 is $0. Withholding was below 90% of 2025 tax and below 100% or 110% of 2024 tax.
findings.why_no: The gate is computed as line 75 > $0, so it is false and the late-or-short question is never asked. Skipping every installment is the most extreme short payment, but the tool treats est_penalty_late as false.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 23, Line 81: "You may owe an estimated tax penalty if you did not have enough tax withheld from your wages or did not make enough estimated tax payments on other income ... You may owe a penalty ... if you underpaid your estimated tax liability for any payment period."
findings.fix: Do not gate on line 75 > 0. Ask everyone whose 2025 prepayments (withholding plus estimated payments) were below the safe harbor (100% of 2024 NY tax, or 110% if 2024 NY AGI was over $150,000, or $75,000 if married filing separately) whether any installment period was unpaid, late or short. Alternatively, compute the per-period underpayment from Form IT-2105.9.

findings.who: A wage earner whose withholding was not enough and who made no estimated payments. Their 2025 balance due on line 80 is $300 or more and is more than 10% of the 2025 income tax shown, and they do not meet the prior-year safe harbor.
findings.why_no: Line 75 is $0, so the gate is false and the penalty pathway is closed. The instructions say a penalty may apply on the line 80 test alone, whether or not any estimated payments were made.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 23, Line 81: "You may owe a penalty: • if line 80 is $300 or more and represents more than 10% of the income tax shown on your 2025 return"
findings.fix: Gate the penalty inquiry on total prepayments being below the safe harbor, or on the line 80 test, not on line 75 > 0.

findings.who: A filer who made estimated payments for only some quarters, for example only in September and January. The payments together reached the year's total, but nothing was paid by the April 15 or June 15 due dates.
findings.why_no: The question asks whether any of 'your 2025 New York estimated payments' was 'made late, or smaller than a quarter'. Each payment actually made was on time and large, so the filer reads a skipped installment as not being 'a payment' and answers no.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 23, Line 81: "if you underpaid your estimated tax liability for any payment period"
findings.fix: Ask: "For any of the four 2025 installment due dates (April 15, June 16, September 15, 2025 and January 15, 2026), did you or your spouse pay less than one quarter of the year's required amount by that date, including paying nothing?"

findings.who: A married couple filing jointly where one spouse made the estimated payments on a separate schedule, or one spouse missed a quarter. The person answering knows only their own payments.
findings.why_no: The question says 'your' estimated payments, and the answering spouse's own payments were on time.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 23, Line 81: "if you underpaid your estimated tax liability for any payment period"
findings.fix: Say "you or your spouse" and refer to combined installments for each due date.

findings.who: A filer who compares each payment with one quarter of the tax they actually paid or expected. The required installment is a quarter of the required annual payment, which is the lesser of 90% of 2025 tax or 100%/110% of 2024 tax, computed on Form IT-2105.9.
findings.why_no: 'Smaller than a quarter of what was due for the year' leaves the filer to work out the required annual payment, and the help text does not explain it. A filer whose income rose may compare against last year's payments and wrongly answer no.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 23, Line 81: "your 2025 prepayments must equal at least 110% of your 2024 New York income tax ... For more information, see Form IT-2105.9"
findings.fix: Collect 2024 NY AGI, 2024 NY tax and the dates and amounts of each payment, then compute the required installments rather than asking the filer to judge them.

used.revision: Form IT-201-I (2025), Instructions for Form IT-201 (including instructions for Forms IT-195 and IT-201-ATT), 41 pages; final 2025 edition; PDF modified 2025-11-20
locators: p. 23, Line 81, "if you underpaid your estimated tax liability for any payment period"

p. 23, Line 81: Penalty for underpaying your tax (estimated tax penalty), "You may owe an estimated tax penalty if you did not have enough tax withheld from your wages or did not make enough estimated tax payments on other income you earned during the year."

findings.who: A married couple filing jointly where only the spouse's employer provided dependent care benefits (for example, through the spouse's dependent care FSA, W-2 box 10), or only the spouse paid the daycare provider from the spouse's own account.
findings.why_no: The gate is computed from the f2441 helpers 'Did you pay for the care of a qualifying person so you could work or look for work?' and 'Did you receive dependent care benefits?', which say only 'you'. The filer truthfully answers no for themselves. The displayed text says 'you (or your spouse)', but the inputs that drive the condition do not.
findings.irs_text: ny_it216i p. 1: 'The care was provided so you (and your spouse, if you were married) could work or look for work.'; 'Caution: Taxpayers who receive dependent care benefits from their employer must complete Worksheet 1 – Dependent care benefits.'
findings.fix: Word both f2441 helpers as 'Did you or your spouse pay for…' and 'Did you or your spouse receive dependent care benefits (for example, Form W-2 box 10 or a dependent care FSA)?', or ask a per-return gate that names the spouse.

findings.who: An employee whose employer paid the care provider directly, ran an on-site daycare, or reimbursed care through a dependent care FSA funded by salary reduction. The employee never handed over money for care and never thinks of having 'received' a benefit.
findings.why_no: 'Did you pay for the care' reads as no because the FSA or employer paid. 'Did you receive dependent care benefits' reads as no because no cash was received, and nothing points the filer to Form W-2 box 10.
findings.irs_text: ny_it216i p. 1: 'Caution: Taxpayers who receive dependent care benefits from their employer must complete Worksheet 1 – Dependent care benefits.'
findings.fix: Add help: 'Include care paid through a dependent care FSA or flexible spending plan, care your employer paid for or provided on site, and any amount in Form W-2 box 10.'

findings.who: A filer who paid for care of a disabled spouse or a disabled adult dependent (for example, a parent living with them) so they could work. Or a filer whose child turned 13 during 2025, with care paid for the months before the birthday.
findings.why_no: 'Care of a qualifying person' and 'child and dependent care' read as childcare for young children. The filer does not see adult care or the part-year care of a child who turned 13 as covered.
findings.irs_text: ny_it216i p. 1: 'Your spouse who is disabled and not able to care for themself and lived with you for more than half the year.'; 'If the child turned 13 during the year, the child is a qualifying person for the part of the year they were under age 13.'
findings.fix: Add help: 'A qualifying person includes a child under 13 (for the part of the year under 13), a disabled spouse, or a disabled person who lived with you more than half the year and whom you claim or could claim as a dependent.'

findings.who: A working parent who paid for summer day camp, a before- or after-school program, preschool or nursery school, or a grandparent or other relative (not a dependent) who babysat while the parents worked.
findings.why_no: These payments are not perceived as 'care expenses'. Camp and after-school programs read as activities, preschool reads as education, and paying a relative reads as informal family help.
findings.irs_text: ny_it216i p. 1: 'The person who provided the care was not your spouse, the parent of your qualifying child under age 13, or a person whom you can claim as a dependent. If your child (including stepchild or foster child) provided the care, they must have been age 19 or older by December 31.'
findings.fix: Add help listing examples: 'daycare, preschool, before/after-school programs, day camp (not overnight camp), and paid babysitters, including relatives who are not your dependents.'

findings.who: A filer who in 2025 paid a provider's bill for care given in late 2024, or who prepaid in 2024 for care provided in 2025.
findings.why_no: A filer who reads the helper as asking about 2025 care paid in 2025 answers no when the payment and the care fall in different years.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 19, Line 64: 'Would you qualify to claim the federal child and dependent care credit for 2025 (whether or not you actually claimed it)?'
findings.fix: Add help: 'Answer yes if you paid in 2025 for care given in an earlier year, or if care given in 2025 was paid earlier.'

locators: p. 1, Who qualifies, "If you qualify to claim the federal child and dependent care credit, you can claim the New York State credit (whether you actually claim the federal credit or not)." and "The care was provided so you (and your spouse, if you were married) could work or look for work." and "Caution: Taxpayers who receive dependent care benefits from their employer must complete Worksheet 1 – Dependent care benefits."

p. 19, Line 64, "Would you qualify to claim the federal child and dependent care credit for 2025 (whether or not you actually claimed it)?"

findings.who: A former New York State, New York City or federal employee who retired on disability before the plan's minimum retirement age. The disability pension is reported as wages (federal Form 1040 line 1h, carried to IT-201 wages), so nothing is on line 9 or 10.
findings.why_no: The helper 'Is there taxable IRA, pension or annuity income on line 9 or 10?' is false. So the government pension question and this follow-up are never asked, even though the payment is a government pension included in federal AGI.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 9, Line 26: 'Did you receive a pension or other distribution from a New York State or local government pension plan or federal government pension plan that was included in your federal adjusted gross income?'
findings.fix: Ask the government pension question whenever any pension, annuity, disability retirement or plan distribution is included in federal AGI, wherever it is reported (wages, line 9 or line 10). Do not tie it only to amounts on lines 9 and 10.

findings.who: A retiree from a local public employer: NYS Teachers' Retirement System, NYC Teachers' or NYC Employees' Retirement System, a school district, BOCES, fire district, public library, police or fire pension fund, or the NYS & Local Retirement System. The retiree does not think of the payer as 'government'.
findings.why_no: They answer no to the government pension question. The follow-up then lists only the MTA, MABSTOA, the LIRR and SUNY/CUNY/SED plans. Its help, 'These public plans count as government pensions', implies those are the only non-obvious cases, so they truthfully answer no again.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 9, Line 26: '– Local governments within the state.' and '– New York State, including State and City University of New York ...'
findings.fix: Broaden the follow-up: 'Was any of it from a public employer's plan, such as NYSLRS, a teachers' retirement system, a New York City retirement system, a school district, fire or police pension fund, the MTA, the LIRR, MABSTOA, or a SUNY, CUNY or State Education Department plan (such as TIAA)?'

findings.who: A military retiree paid by DFAS, a federal civil service annuitant paid by OPM (CSRS/FERS), or a retiree of a U.S. territory, U.S. agency or the District of Columbia government.
findings.why_no: They read 'retired pay' or an OPM 'annuity' as not a 'pension'. Also, the follow-up names only New York public bodies, so a federal payer never matches it.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 9, Line 26: '– The United States, its territories, possessions ... or any agency or instrumentality of the United States (including the military), or the District of Columbia.'
findings.fix: Add to the follow-up: 'military retired pay (DFAS), a federal civil service annuity (OPM), or a pension from a U.S. territory, a U.S. agency or the District of Columbia government'.

findings.who: A surviving spouse or other beneficiary receiving a survivor annuity from a government plan. Or an ex-spouse paid under a QDRO, or a New York DRO, from a NYS, local or federal plan.
findings.why_no: They think 'a pension' means their own pension from their own work. A survivor benefit, or an ex-spouse's pension split by court order, does not seem to count. Neither question mentions beneficiaries or court orders.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 9, Line 26: 'as an officer, employee, or beneficiary of an officer or employee' and 'You may include distributions you received ... as a nonemployee spouse in accordance with a court-issued qualified domestic relations order (QDRO)'
findings.fix: Add to both questions: 'including survivor or beneficiary payments, and payments to you under a divorce or domestic relations order'.

findings.who: A person who left New York public employment before retiring and took a refund of their pension contributions, part of which was taxable.
findings.why_no: They see it as a refund of their own money, not a pension they 'received'. The follow-up again asks only about a pension 'from' named plans.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 9, Line 26: 'or any distributions made to you from a pension plan that represents a return of contributions in a year prior to retirement'
findings.fix: Ask 'Did you receive a pension, a refund of your contributions, or any other payment from a government retirement plan ...'.

findings.why_no: The government pension question and its follow-up say 'you' and 'any of it' with no mention of the spouse, so the filer answers about their own income.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 9, Line 26: 'Did you receive a pension or other distribution from a New York State or local government pension plan or federal government pension plan ...'
findings.fix: Say 'Did you or your spouse receive ...' in both the government pension question and the follow-up.

findings.who: A college student, or the student's parents on a joint return, received in 2025 a withdrawal from a New York 529 account that a grandparent owns. Part of the withdrawal was non-qualified and was included in the student's federal AGI.
findings.why_no: The help says 'an account someone else owns for you counts as No', and the question asks only about accounts 'you (or your spouse) own'. A beneficiary who is not the owner truthfully answers No. The federal gate question ('had a 529 plan... account') also invites a No from someone who does not own the account.
findings.line: ny_it201.ny_529_if_account (and the line 30 beneficiary subtraction it controls)
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 10, Line 30, Beneficiary: 'During 2025, did you, as a beneficiary, receive a withdrawal from one or more tuition savings accounts established under New York's 529 college savings program? ... If Yes, and you included part of the withdrawal in your federal adjusted gross income ... then enter that amount on line 30.'
findings.fix: Add a separate gate and question for beneficiaries: 'In 2025, did you (or your spouse) receive a withdrawal from a New York 529 College Savings Program account, including one owned by someone else, such as a parent or grandparent?' Remove 'an account someone else owns for you counts as No' from the help, or limit it to the owner contribution and withdrawal part.

findings.who: An account owner who withdrew everything from a New York 529 account in 2025, or rolled it out, and closed it. Part of the withdrawal was included in federal AGI.
findings.why_no: The question is in the present tense ('Is any 529 account you ... own part of New York's ... program?'). An owner who no longer owns any account at filing time reads it as No.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 10, Line 30: 'During 2025, did you, as an account owner, make contributions to or a withdrawal from one or more tuition savings accounts established under New York's 529 college savings program?'
findings.fix: Ask in the instruction's own terms: 'During 2025, did you (or your spouse), as an account owner, contribute to or withdraw from a New York 529 College Savings Program account, even if the account is now closed?'

findings.who: A New York account owner who made 2025 contributions only. They took no distribution and received no Form 1099-Q, so nothing on the federal return concerns the 529.
findings.why_no: The gate is computed from a federal answer. A federal question about 529, Coverdell or ABLE accounts is typically driven by distributions or Form 1099-Q, which a contribution-only owner does not have. They answer No, and the New York question about contributions is never asked.
findings.line: ny_it201.ny_529_if_account (line 30 worksheet line 1, contributions up to $5,000/$10,000)
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 10, Line 30 worksheet line 1: 'Amount of contributions you made in 2025 to an account established under New York's 529 college savings program (cannot exceed $5,000 ... or $10,000 for married taxpayers filing a joint return)'
findings.fix: Do not gate the New York question on the federal answer. Ask the New York line 30 question directly of every New York resident filer. If a federal gate is kept, word it as 'own, contribute to, or receive a withdrawal from', and make clear that contributions alone count.

findings.who: A New York resident whose account is in New York's Advisor-Guided 529 plan, opened through a financial advisor, rather than the Direct Plan.
findings.why_no: The help names only 'the New York 529 College Savings Program'. An owner whose statements carry an advisor or brokerage brand may decide their plan is not 'New York's own' and answer No.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 10, Line 30: 'one or more tuition savings accounts established under New York's 529 college savings program'
findings.fix: Help: 'New York's program includes both the Direct Plan and the Advisor-Guided Plan, including accounts opened through a financial advisor. A 529 plan sponsored by another state counts as No.'

findings.who: A filer holds Federal Home Loan Bank or Federal Farm Credit Bank bonds, or Tennessee Valley Authority notes. Their interest is on line 2 and has no Treasury or savings bond component.
findings.why_no: The question lists only 'U.S. Treasury bills, notes or bonds, U.S. savings bonds, or a fund that holds them'. Agency bonds are none of these, so the filer truthfully answers No.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 9, Line 28: 'Did you include interest income from U.S. government bonds or other U.S. government obligations on lines 2, 6, or 11?'
findings.fix: Ask: 'Was any of your (or your spouse's) interest or dividends, including amounts passed through from a business, partnership, S corporation, estate or trust, from the U.S. government or a U.S. government agency? Examples are Treasury bills, notes or bonds, savings bonds, federal agency bonds, or a fund that holds them.' Classify after a broad yes.

findings.who: A married couple files jointly. Only the spouse owns Treasury bonds, U.S. savings bonds, or Build America Bonds, and the filer answers the tool's questions.
findings.why_no: The question as shown reads 'Was any of your interest or dividends from...' without 'or your spouse's'. The filer reads 'your' as their own holdings. The helper text names the spouse, but the question shown does not.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 9, Line 28: 'Did you include interest income from U.S. government bonds or other U.S. government obligations on lines 2, 6, or 11?'; ny_it201i p. 5, Item G Code A6: 'Enter this code if you included Build America Bond interest in your federal adjusted gross income.'
findings.fix: Say 'you or your spouse' in both gated questions on a joint return.

findings.who: A partner, S corporation shareholder, or trust beneficiary receives a Schedule K-1 that reports U.S. Treasury interest or Build America Bond interest. That interest flows into line 11, or into line 6 as part of business income.
findings.why_no: The filer received no Form 1099-INT for it. The question asks about 'your interest or dividends' and the help points to 'box 3 of a Form 1099-INT'. The filer thinks of K-1 or business income as something other than their interest.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 9, Line 28: '...on lines 2, 6, or 11?' and 'If you include an amount on line 28 from more than one line on Form IT-201, submit a schedule...'
findings.fix: Add to both questions: 'including interest reported to you on a Schedule K-1 or earned in your business'. Mention Schedule K-1 in the help.

findings.who: A filer's Schedule C or Schedule E nets to exactly $0, so line 6 or line 11 is $0, and lines 2 and 3 are also $0. The netted business or partnership income still includes Treasury interest or Build America Bond interest.
findings.why_no: The computed gate tests whether each line is nonzero. A component of a line that nets to zero leaves the gate false, so neither question is asked.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 9, Line 28: 'Did you include interest income from U.S. government bonds or other U.S. government obligations on lines 2, 6, or 11?'
findings.fix: Also open the gate when any Schedule C, Schedule E or K-1 is present, whatever the net amount on line 6 or line 11.

findings.who: A filer who reported the New York inflation refund check on federal Schedule 1, line 1 (taxable refunds, credits, or offsets of state and local income taxes) rather than as other income. That line is where the check most naturally goes, and where software that treats it as a state refund puts it. They have no entries on lines 8a through 8z, so Schedule 1 line 9 is $0.
findings.why_no: The computed gate tests only Schedule 1 line 9 (total other income). Line 1 is not part of line 9, so the gate is false and the inflation-check question is never asked. Even if the gate were broadened, the question asks whether 'any of the other income' was the check, and this filer truthfully says no because they reported it as a refund, not other income.
findings.line: ny_it201.inflation_if_other_income (and so the Yes that ends the New York part, plus IT-201 line 25)
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 8, Line 25 heading 'Taxable refunds, credits, or offsets of state and local income taxes': 'If you received an inflation refund check from the Tax Department and included the check amount in the calculation of federal adjusted gross income reported on line 19, then enter that amount on line 25.'
findings.fix: Gate on any check included in federal AGI, not on Schedule 1 line 9. Ask whenever Schedule 1 line 1 or line 9 is non-zero, or ask unconditionally: 'Did you (or your spouse) receive a New York State inflation refund check and report it anywhere on your federal return, for example as a state tax refund (Schedule 1, line 1) or as other income (Schedule 1, line 8z)?'

findings.who: A filer whose Schedule 1 line 9 is non-zero for another reason (for example, gambling winnings or a prize), and who also included the inflation check in federal AGI.
findings.why_no: The question asks whether the check was part of the 'other income you reported.' A filer who thinks of the check as a refund or rebate of their own tax, rather than as income, reads it as not 'other income' and answers no, although it is in federal AGI.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 8, Line 25: 'If you received an inflation refund check from the Tax Department and included the check amount in the calculation of federal adjusted gross income ... enter that amount on line 25.'
findings.fix: Ask about the fact, not the classification: 'Did you include any New York inflation refund check in the income on your federal return, whether as a refund or as other income?'

findings.who: Married filers on a joint return where the inflation refund check was issued in the spouse's name (based on the spouse's earlier return) and included in the joint federal AGI.
findings.why_no: The gated question says 'you reported' with no mention of a spouse. A filer who did not personally receive the check may answer no, even though the helper covers 'you (or, on a joint return, your spouse).'
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 8, Line 25: 'If you received an inflation refund check from the Tax Department and included the check amount in the calculation of federal adjusted gross income ...'
findings.fix: Word the question as 'Did you or your spouse receive a New York State inflation refund check ...'

findings.who: A filer whose Schedule 1 other-income entries net to exactly $0, for example a positive line 8z amount equal to a line 8a net operating loss, with the inflation check among the positive entries.
findings.why_no: The computed test 'line 9 ≠ $0' is false when other-income items offset each other, so the question is not asked.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 8, Line 25: 'included the check amount in the calculation of federal adjusted gross income reported on line 19'
findings.fix: Gate on the presence of any Schedule 1 line 1 or line 8 entry, not on the net total on line 9.

findings.who: A New York City or Yonkers resident, or a self-employed filer in the MCTD who owes MCTMT. They want this year's overpayment credited to their 2026 city, Yonkers, or MCTMT estimated tax.
findings.why_no: The question says "your 2026 New York tax" and the help says "New York estimated tax". A filer may read this as New York State income tax only, so they answer no and plan to pay the city, Yonkers, or MCTMT estimate separately.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 23, Line 79: "Enter the amount of overpayment from line 77 that you want applied to your New York State, New York City, Yonkers, and metropolitan commuter transportation mobility tax estimated tax for 2026."
findings.fix: Ask: "Do you or your spouse want any of your New York overpayment applied to your 2026 New York State, New York City, Yonkers, or MCTMT estimated tax instead of refunded?"

findings.who: Spouses filing a joint return. One spouse makes the 2026 estimated payments, and the other spouse answers the tool's questions.
findings.why_no: The question asks whether "you" want "your" refund kept. The answering spouse does not plan to pay estimated tax and answers no for the couple.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 23, Line 79: "Enter the amount of overpayment from line 77 that you want applied to your ... estimated tax for 2026."
findings.fix: Say "you or your spouse" on joint returns.

findings.who: A filer with an overpayment on line 77 who plans to direct part of it to NYS 529 accounts on line 78a. They see the rest as a credit, not a "refund".
findings.why_no: The question uses the word "refund", but line 78 is the refund that remains after line 79 is taken out. A filer who expects no check may think they have no "refund" to keep.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 23, Line 78: "Subtract the amount on line 79 (estimated tax) from line 77. This is the amount available for refund."
findings.fix: Use "overpayment (line 77)" in place of "refund". Show the line 77 amount in the question.

findings.who: A retired New York City police officer or firefighter, or a federal or military employee, receives a government disability pension before reaching the plan's minimum retirement age. Following the federal rule, the taxable amount is reported as wages on federal Form 1040 line 1 (so on IT-201 line 1), not as pensions and annuities. Nothing else of theirs lands on line 9 or 10.
findings.why_no: The computed gate checks only lines 9 and 10. Lines 9 and 10 are zero, so the condition is false, the government pension question is never asked, and the line 26 subtraction is silently zero even though the pension is in federal AGI.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 9, Line 26: "Did you receive a pension or other distribution from a New York State or local government pension plan or federal government pension plan that was included in your federal adjusted gross income?" (the test is inclusion in federal AGI, not on line 9 or 10)
findings.fix: Do not gate on lines 9/10 alone. Ask the government pension question whenever the filer or spouse received any Form 1099-R or any pension or disability retirement payment, including amounts reported as wages on line 1. Alternatively, add to the gate: 'or any government disability pension reported as wages before minimum retirement age'.

findings.who: A retired Long Island Rail Road worker, a MABSTOA bus operator, or an MTA Police 20-Year Retirement Program retiree, filing alone or jointly, whose pension is on line 10.
findings.why_no: The question names 'the federal government, the military, or a New York State or local government job'. The help does not mention public authorities. A railroad or transit-authority retiree reasonably does not see the LIRR or MABSTOA as a 'government job' and answers no.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 9, Line 26: "Certain public authorities, including: • Metropolitan Transit Authority (MTA) Police 20-Year Retirement Program; • Manhattan and Bronx Surface Transit Operating Authority (MABSTOA); and • Long Island Railroad Company."
findings.fix: Name these in the question or help: 'Count the MTA Police 20-Year Retirement Program, MABSTOA, and the Long Island Rail Road.' The gate helper already lists them; carry that list into the filer-facing question.

findings.who: A retired SUNY or CUNY professor, or a former State Education Department employee, in the Optional Retirement Program. The annuity is paid and reported on Form 1099-R by TIAA, a private company.
findings.why_no: The payer on the form is TIAA, not a government. The filer thinks of it as a TIAA annuity, not 'pension or retirement money from a New York State or local government job', and answers no.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 9, Line 26: "New York State, including State and City University of New York and New York State Education Department employees who belong to the Optional Retirement Program."
findings.fix: Add to the help: 'Count the Optional Retirement Program of SUNY, CUNY or the State Education Department, even when the payer is TIAA or another private company (only the part from that employment).'

findings.who: A New York resident who receives a pension from former government employment in Puerto Rico, Guam, the U.S. Virgin Islands, or the District of Columbia.
findings.why_no: The question lists only 'the federal government, the military, or a New York State or local government job'. A territorial or D.C. government pension is none of these on a plain reading, so the filer answers no.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 9, Line 26: "The United States, its territories, possessions (or political subdivisions thereof), or any agency or instrumentality of the United States (including the military), or the District of Columbia."
findings.fix: Add to the question: 'a U.S. territory or possession (or one of its local governments), or the District of Columbia'.

findings.who: A former New York State or local employee, or a former federal employee, who left the job before retirement and this year took a refund of their own pension contributions (reported on line 10). They have never retired.
findings.why_no: The question asks about 'pension or retirement money'. The help mentions 'a refund of your own contributions', but a filer who never retired may not connect a contribution refund on leaving a job with 'pension' money and answers no.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 9, Line 26: "any distributions made to you from a pension plan that represents a return of contributions in a year prior to retirement"
findings.fix: Put it in the question itself: 'including a refund of your own pension contributions when you left the job, even if you never retired'.

findings.who: A filer with an overpayment on line 77 who is first asked how much of it to apply to 2026 estimated tax and enters the whole overpayment, planning to direct part of it to a 529 account later. Line 78 then computes as zero.
findings.why_no: No answer from the filer is involved; the gate is computed. If the tool asks for the line 79 amount before the 529 question, a full line 79 entry makes line 78 zero, and the 529 question is never shown. The filer never sees that line 78a and line 79 compete for the same line 77 overpayment.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 23, Line 79: "Enter the amount of overpayment from line 77 that you want applied to your ... estimated tax for 2026. The total of lines 78a through 79 should equal the amount on line 77."; Line 78: "Subtract the amount on line 79 (estimated tax) from line 77."
findings.fix: Ask about the 529 deposit (or base the gate on line 77 > $0) before asking for the line 79 amount, or say in the line 79 question that any amount applied to estimated tax cannot also go to a 529 account or be refunded.

findings.who: A filer who bought out-of-state municipal bonds at a large premium, for example high-coupon bonds bought near a call date. The 1099-INT box 13 amortizable premium on tax-exempt bonds offsets the box 8 interest, so the net tax-exempt interest reported on federal line 2a is $0.
findings.why_no: The gate is computed as f1040 line 2a > $0. Federal reporting nets premium amortization against tax-exempt interest, so line 2a can be zero. The tool then never asks the question, even though gross interest was received.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 7, Line 20: "For purposes of this addition, bond premium amortization is not allowed as a direct offset to interest income. You must report it: • as a subtraction modification on Form IT-225 ... or • as an itemized deduction addition adjustment on Form IT-196, line 44"
findings.fix: Base the gate on the gross figure: line 2a > 0 OR any 1099-INT box 8 or box 13 amount OR any 1099-DIV box 12 amount. Or ask directly whether the filer or spouse held any state or local bonds, or tax-exempt funds, at any time in 2025.

findings.who: A filer who sold an out-of-state municipal bond between interest dates in 2025, before any coupon was paid to them that year. The accrued interest was received as part of the sale price and went into proceeds rather than into tax-exempt interest on line 2a, so line 2a is $0.
findings.why_no: The computed condition line 2a > $0 is false, so the question is never asked. The accrued interest received on the sale is a sale-date event, not a reported interest payment.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 7, Line 20: "If you sold a bond between interest dates, include the amount of interest you received during the year plus the accrued interest amount ... to the date you sold the bond."
findings.fix: Add a gate branch for any sale or redemption of a state or local bond in 2025 (Form 1099-B or a brokerage statement), and ask for the accrued interest received at sale.

findings.who: A partner or S corporation shareholder whose K-1 reports out-of-state municipal interest (partnership box 18A, S corporation box 16A, plus the NY modification EA-113 from the entity). The filer or tool did not carry it to federal line 2a, which is common because it has no federal tax effect.
findings.why_no: The gate is computed only from line 2a. Entity-level tax-exempt interest that never reached line 2a leaves the gate false. The NY instructions route the entity's EA-113 amount directly to line 20.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 7: "If you have either of the addition or subtraction modifications in the chart below, relating to your partnership or S corporation income, include the amount on the corresponding line of Form IT-201. ... EA-113 Interest income on state and local bonds and obligations 20"
findings.fix: Also open the gate when any partnership or S corporation K-1 (yours or your spouse's) reports tax-exempt interest or an EA-113 modification. Ask: 'Did a partnership or S corporation report a New York modification EA-113 to you or your spouse?'

findings.who: A joint filer whose spouse alone holds a national tax-free bond fund or out-of-state bonds, while the asker holds only New York bonds.
findings.why_no: The gated question reads "Did any of your tax-free interest or dividends come from bonds issued outside New York". The spouse is named only in the helper wording, not in the question actually asked, so the asker answers for their own holdings.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 7, Line 20: "enter any such interest income that you received or that was credited to you during 2025 that was not included in your federal adjusted gross income."
findings.fix: Reword: "Did any tax-free interest or dividends received by you or, on a joint return, your spouse come from bonds issued outside New York, or from a fund that holds them?"

findings.who: A filer holding a 'New York tax-free' municipal bond fund whose year-end statement shows that part of its exempt-interest dividends came from non-New York issuers, for example 5% from other states' bonds.
findings.why_no: The help says "Bonds of New York State, its cities and agencies ... count as No" and contrasts "national tax-free bond funds". A holder of a fund named New York reads it as entirely New York and answers No.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 7, Line 20: "This includes interest income on: ... interest and dividend income from tax-exempt bond mutual funds, and – tax-exempt money market funds that invest in obligations of states other than New York."
findings.fix: Add to the help: "A New York tax-free fund may still hold some bonds of other states or of territories; check the fund's year-end statement for the percentage from New York. Answer Yes if any part is from other states."

findings.who: A filer who received a small amount of out-of-state municipal interest with no 1099-INT, for example under $10, or interest on a directly held bond. They did not enter it on line 2a.
findings.why_no: The gate depends on line 2a having been filled from information returns. Without a form, the amount never reaches line 2a and the question is never asked.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 7, Line 20: "enter any such interest income that you received or that was credited to you during 2025"
findings.fix: Ask about holdings of state or local bonds or tax-exempt funds, whether or not a form was received, rather than relying solely on line 2a.

findings.who: A married couple filing jointly with FAGI of $15,000. The house they live in is titled only to the spouse, is worth $70,000, and the spouse pays its property taxes. The filer named first on the return owns no real estate and pays no rent.
findings.why_no: The question asks whether 'your rent' was $450 or less, or whether 'all the real estate you own' is worth $85,000 or less. The first filer pays no rent and owns no real estate, so they truthfully answer no.
findings.line: ny_it201.gate.real_property (Form IT-201 line 67 / Form IT-214 never prompted)
findings.irs_text: ny_it214i p. 1: 'Homeowners – You or your spouse (if married filing jointly) paid real property taxes.' ... 'Renters – You or your spouse (if married filing jointly) paid rent for your residence.'
findings.fix: Ask: 'Did you or your spouse pay rent averaging $450 a month or less, or own real estate (all of it together) worth $85,000 or less, for your New York home?'

findings.who: A renter in a furnished room who pays $520 a month. The landlord's charge includes $100 a month for furnishings, so the adjusted rent is $420.
findings.why_no: The question says to leave out only 'heat, gas, electricity or meals'. It does not mention furnishings, so the filer counts the full $520 and answers no.
findings.irs_text: ny_it214i p. 1: 'The average monthly rent ... was $450 or less, not counting charges for heat, gas, electricity, furnishings, or board.'; p. 2 Line 12: 'Adjusted rent is the rent paid after subtracting any charges for heat, gas, electricity, furnishings, and board.'
findings.fix: List all five exclusions: 'not counting charges for heat, gas, electricity, furnishings, or board (meals)'.

findings.who: A Section 8 or other subsidized tenant. The lease rent is $1,100 a month, but the tenant pays only their own share of $300 a month.
findings.why_no: The filer reads 'your rent' as the lease or contract rent of $1,100 and answers no. The instructions count only the part the filer paid, with the subsidized part excluded.
findings.irs_text: ny_it214i p. 2 Line 11: 'Enter the total rent you or your spouse ... paid during 2025; do not include any subsidized part of your rental charge.'
findings.fix: Ask about 'the rent you or your spouse paid yourselves (not counting any part paid by a housing subsidy)'.

findings.who: A tenant-stockholder in a New York cooperative whose shares are worth under $85,000. Monthly maintenance is $600, which includes the share of real estate taxes deductible under IRC section 216.
findings.why_no: The filer owns shares rather than 'real estate', so they say they own none. They also treat the $600 maintenance as rent above $450. The gate's help text mentions only 'rent or property tax', and they do not see maintenance as either.
findings.irs_text: ny_it214i p. 2: 'A condominium, a cooperative, or a rental unit within a single dwelling is also a residence.' ... 'Real property taxes paid also include any real estate taxes allowed ... as a deduction for tenant-stockholders in a cooperative housing corporation under IRC section 216.'
findings.fix: Add a branch: 'Do you or your spouse own a co-op or condo unit (count co-op shares as real estate)?' Also say that co-op maintenance includes property tax.

findings.who: A homeowner who lived in and paid taxes on a $70,000 house from January to October 2025, then sold it. They now rent an apartment at $600 a month and own no real estate.
findings.why_no: The present tense 'is all the real estate you own' points to today, when they own nothing, so they answer not applicable or no. The rent half is also false. Yet they paid 2025 property taxes on a residence they occupied for at least six months.
findings.irs_text: ny_it214i p. 2 Line 15: 'Real property taxes paid are all current, prior, and prepaid real property taxes ... levied upon a residence owned or previously owned by a qualified taxpayer ... and paid during the tax year.'; Line 18: 'If you owned your residence for part of the tax year and rented your residence for part of the tax year, add the amount from line 17 to the amount from line 14.'
findings.fix: Use the past tense and the whole year: 'At any time in 2025, did you or your spouse own and live in a New York home where all your real estate was worth $85,000 or less, or rent one for an average of $450 a month or less?'

findings.who: A renter who moved during 2025, from a $520-a-month apartment to a $350-a-month apartment where they lived for seven months.
findings.why_no: 'Was your rent $450 a month or less' does not say which apartment or which period counts. The filer remembers the $520 rent, or a year average above $450, and answers no. The instructions add adjusted rent across residences, and the six-month residence may qualify on its own.
findings.irs_text: ny_it214i p. 2 Line 12: 'If you moved from one rented residence to another rented residence, calculate the adjusted rent for each residence. Add the total adjusted rent for all rented residences and enter on line 12.'
findings.fix: Add: 'If you moved, answer yes if the home you lived in for six months or more had rent of $450 a month or less.'

findings.who: A general partner or member of an LLC taxed as a partnership, such as a Manhattan law-firm partner, with $200,000 of net earnings from self-employment reported on Schedule K-1 and no Schedule C. On a joint return, the spouse may be the partner.
findings.why_no: The gate is computed from Schedule C alone: more than one Schedule C, or Schedule C net profit over $50,000. With no Schedule C the count is zero, the gate is false, and the MCTMT question is never asked.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 15: "For purposes of the MCTMT, self-employed individuals include: • Sole proprietors • Partners in partnerships • Members of limited liability companies (LLCs) that are treated as partnerships • Partners of limited liability partnerships (LLPs)"
findings.fix: Count a person in the helper if they have any partnership or LLC self-employment earnings (federal Schedule K-1, box 14, code A), or Schedule SE net earnings over $50,000. Simpler: ask whether you or your spouse had any self-employment or partnership earnings from business in the MCTD.

findings.who: A sole proprietor with one Schedule C showing $40,000 net profit in Queens who is also a partner with $30,000 of K-1 self-employment earnings from a Brooklyn partnership. The Zone 1 base from both sources is $70,000.
findings.why_no: The person has exactly one Schedule C and it is under $50,000. The partnership source is not counted, so the gate is false.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 15: "You must calculate your MCTMT net earnings base separately for each source of self-employment income ... If you have more than one source, combine all the individual amounts on line 54a (Zone 1 amounts) or line 54b (Zone 2 amounts)"
findings.fix: Make the helper test the combined self-employment earnings for each person across all sources (Schedule C, Schedule F, and partnership K-1), not the count or size of Schedule C forms.

findings.who: A Suffolk or Orange County farmer whose Schedule F shows $90,000 of net farm profit and who has no Schedule C.
findings.why_no: The helper looks only at Schedule C. Farm income goes on Schedule F but is still net earnings from self-employment, so the gate is false.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 15: "If an individual’s net earnings from self-employment allocated to either zone exceed $50,000 for the tax year, then you are subject to the MCTMT."
findings.fix: Base the helper on each person's Schedule SE net earnings from self-employment, which covers Schedule C, Schedule F and partnership earnings. Do not base it on Schedule C.

findings.who: A Connecticut-resident partner in a Manhattan partnership, or a consultant whose own office is in New Jersey but whose business is allocated partly to NYC.
findings.why_no: The question asks whether earnings "come from business done in New York City or the nearby counties." The filer thinks of their own work as done elsewhere and does not see that the partnership's or business's allocation percentage puts the earnings in a zone.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 15: "To calculate your MCTMT net earnings base you must multiply your net earnings from self-employment from each source by the specific zone’s allocation percentage for each source"
findings.fix: Ask whether any business or partnership you or your spouse earned self-employment income from had business activity in the five NYC boroughs or the listed counties, wherever you live or work. Then compute or ask the allocated amount.

findings.who: A full-year New York State resident who lives outside New York City, such as in Buffalo, Albany or Westchester. They either moved in from another state at the start of 2025 or are leaving New York State at the start of 2026, and they have a bonus earned in 2025 but paid in 2026.
findings.why_no: The computed gate asks only whether they moved into or out of New York City. They never lived in the City, so both helpers are truthfully false and the special-accrual question is never asked.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 31: "Full-year New York State residents You are subject to the special accrual rules only if you have accrued income for 2025 and • you were a nonresident of New York State on December 31, 2024; or • you will be a New York State nonresident on January 1, 2026."
findings.fix: Broaden the gate to: "(you or your spouse) was a New York State or New York City nonresident on December 31, 2024, became a New York City resident or nonresident during 2025, or will be a New York State or New York City nonresident on January 1, 2026."

findings.who: A full-year New York State resident who was a New York City part-year resident in 2025. For example, they moved from Westchester to Brooklyn in June 2025, or from Manhattan to Long Island in September 2025. They have income fixed and determinable in one period but reportable in the other, or a bonus earned in 2025 and paid in 2026.
findings.why_no: The gate asks only about a move "at the start of 2025" or "at the start of 2026" (January 1). A mid-year move truthfully makes both helpers false.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 31: "Full-year and part-year New York City residents You are subject to the special accrual rules only if you have accrued income for 2025 ... and you were a: ... • New York City part-year resident for tax year 2025."
findings.fix: Add to the gate: "Did you (or your spouse) move into or out of New York City at any time during 2025?" Treat a yes as reaching the special-accrual question.

findings.who: Married couple filing jointly. Only one spouse moved into New York City (or New York State) at the start of 2025, or will leave at the start of 2026, and that spouse has accrued income. The other spouse had no move.
findings.why_no: The helpers "Moved into New York City on January 1, 2025" and "Moved out of New York City on January 1, 2026" do not say "you or your spouse". The filer answering for themselves says no.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 31: "you may have to use special accrual rules ... If you are subject to the special accrual rules, see the instructions for Form IT-225, addition modification number A-115 and subtraction modification number S-129."
findings.fix: Word both helpers as "Did you (or, on a joint return, your spouse) ...".

findings.who: A filer who moved into New York City and New York State on January 1, 2025. In 2025 they report federally some non-New York source income that was fixed and determinable in 2022 or 2023, such as deferred compensation or a lump sum from a former out-of-state employer.
findings.why_no: The question asks about income "earned in one year but paid in the other", and the example is 2025/2026. The filer reads "the other" year as only 2024 or 2026, so income fixed in 2022 or 2023 seems excluded.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 31: "non-New York source income that was fixed and determinable in a tax year prior to 2025, but you are reporting that income for federal income tax purposes in tax year 2025"
findings.fix: Ask: "Do you (or your spouse) report any income in 2025 that became fixed (earned, sold or owed to you) in any earlier year? Or was any income fixed in 2025 that you will report in a later year?"

findings.who: A filer who moved at the year boundary and has accrued income that is not wages or a bonus. Examples: installment-sale gain from an out-of-state property sold before the move, collected and reported in 2025; or a 2025 sale whose gain will be reported in a later year under the installment method.
findings.why_no: The words "earned" and "paid", and the bonus example, suggest compensation. A sale gain or an installment receivable does not feel "earned", and the trigger is when the income is reported federally, not when it is paid.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 31: "income that was fixed and determinable in tax year 2025, but you will be reporting that income for federal income tax purposes in a tax year after 2025"
findings.fix: Use "fixed and determinable" and "reported on your federal return" in plain words, and give more examples in the help: installment sales, deferred compensation, accrued interest, and sale proceeds received in another year.

findings.who: A New York City part-year resident who moved during 2025 (once the gate is broadened). They have income fixed and determinable in the 2025 City resident period but reportable federally in the 2025 nonresident period, or the reverse.
findings.why_no: The question asks only about income "earned in one year but paid in the other". Both dates fall in 2025, so the filer truthfully answers no.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 31: "income that was fixed and determinable in your 2025 New York City resident period, but that income is not reportable for federal income tax purposes in your 2025 New York City resident period"
findings.fix: For filers who moved into or out of New York City during 2025, add: "or became fixed while you lived in the City but is reported for a period when you did not, or the reverse?"

p. 31, Special accruals, "you may have to use special accrual rules (see below) to calculate your New York State and New York City personal income tax for 2025"

findings.who: A parent who emptied or closed their New York 529 account in 2025, either with a cash withdrawal or a full rollover to another state's plan. On December 31 they no longer own any New York 529 account.
findings.why_no: The helper "Owns an account in New York's 529 college savings program" is in the present tense. With the account closed, the truthful answer is no, so neither gated question is asked.
findings.line: ny_it201.gate.line22 (and ny_it201.gate.line30 for contributions made before the account was closed)
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 8, Line 22: "Nonqualified withdrawals ... include ... the transfer to another state's program"; p. 10, Line 30: "During 2025, did you, as an account owner, make contributions to or a withdrawal from..."
findings.fix: Ask "At any time during 2025, did you or your spouse own a New York 529 college savings account, including one closed or rolled to another state's plan during the year?"

findings.who: A college student who is the designated beneficiary, not the owner, of a parent's or grandparent's New York 529 account. They received a 2025 withdrawal, and part of it is included in their federal AGI.
findings.why_no: The gate asks whether they own a New York 529 account. They are only the beneficiary, so they truthfully answer no, and line 30 never reaches the beneficiary branch its own helper describes.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 10, Line 30: "Beneficiary During 2025, did you, as a beneficiary, receive a withdrawal ... If Yes, and you included part of the withdrawal in your federal adjusted gross income ... enter that amount on line 30."
findings.fix: Broaden the gate to "Did you or your spouse own a New York 529 account, or receive a withdrawal from one as its beneficiary, during 2025?" Ask the beneficiary-withdrawal question separately.

findings.who: A married couple filing jointly where only the spouse owns the New York 529 account. The spouse contributed $8,000 or took a nonqualified withdrawal.
findings.why_no: The ownership helper and both gated questions say "you", with no mention of a spouse. The filer answering truthfully says no.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 10, Line 30: "up to $5,000 ($10,000 for married taxpayers filing a joint return)"; ny_it225i p. 8, A-103: "include the applicable amounts from all existing accounts owned by you and your spouse"
findings.fix: Say "you or your spouse" in the ownership helper and in both gated questions, as the line 22 helper already does.

findings.who: An account owner who only contributed to a New York 529 account in 2025. There was no distribution, so no Form 1099-Q, and nothing about the account appears on the federal return.
findings.why_no: The outer helper "A 529 plan, Coverdell or ABLE account on the return" reads as asking whether the federal return reports such an account. Contributions are not reported federally, so the filer answers no and the ownership question is never asked.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 10, Line 30: "as an account owner, made contributions, enter the amount up to $5,000 ... on line 1 of the Line 30 worksheet"
findings.fix: Ask about owning or contributing to a 529, Coverdell or ABLE account whether or not a form was received. Do not tie it to the federal return.

findings.who: An account owner who withdrew from the New York 529 account in spring 2025 to pay the beneficiary's credentialing or career-training costs before July 4, 2025.
findings.why_no: The question excludes money taken out "for ... career training" without a date. The filer truthfully says the money went to career training and answers no.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 8, Line 22: "to pay the qualified postsecondary credentialing expenses of the designated beneficiary at an eligible educational institution on or after July 4, 2025"
findings.fix: Say "career training paid to an eligible school on or after July 4, 2025"; or ask what the money paid for, with dates, and classify after.

findings.who: An account owner who paid credentialing costs to a provider that is not an eligible educational institution. Or one who paid their own Parent PLUS loan, or a loan of someone other than the beneficiary or the beneficiary's sibling.
findings.why_no: The question lists "college, career training or student loans" as qualified without limits. The filer reads their use as one of those and answers no.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 8, Line 22: "any withdrawal used for postsecondary credentialing expenses that are not paid to an eligible educational institution"; "qualified education loan ... of the designated beneficiary or a sibling of the designated beneficiary"
findings.fix: State the limits: "career training paid to an eligible school; student loans of the beneficiary or a sibling of the beneficiary". Otherwise ask the use and the payee, and classify in the tool.

findings.who: An account owner who withdrew more than the beneficiary's qualified college costs, for example after a scholarship or tuition refund, and kept the excess.
findings.why_no: The withdrawal was made "for college", so the filer does not see the unspent excess as money taken out for anything else.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 8, Line 22: "A withdrawal ... is considered nonqualified unless it is used: to pay the qualified higher education expenses of the designated beneficiary at an eligible educational institution"
findings.fix: Add to the help: "Any part not actually spent on those costs (for example, an amount more than tuition after a scholarship) counts as Yes."

findings.who: A filer who owns several New York 529 accounts and was active in a different account from the one they had in mind.
findings.why_no: Both questions refer to "that New York 529 account", in the singular.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 10, Line 30: "contributions to or a withdrawal from one or more tuition savings accounts"
findings.fix: Say "any of your (or your spouse's) New York 529 accounts".

findings.who: A filer, or a spouse on a joint return, born between January 1 and July 1, 1966, who received a taxable IRA, 401(k) or private pension distribution in the second half of 2025, after turning 59½ during the year.
findings.why_no: The gate counts only recipients born in 1965 or earlier. Its helper text claims that this means '59½ or older at some time in 2025', but a person born in the first half of 1966 reaches 59½ between July and December 2025. The computed count is therefore 0, and that person is never asked.
findings.line: ny_it201.pension_exclusion_if_young (and the line 29 exclusion or refusal it leads to)
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 9, Line 29: 'If you became 59½ during 2025, enter only the amount you received after you became 59½, but not more than $20,000.'
findings.fix: Count recipients born before July 2, 1966, not 'in 1965 or earlier'. Better, ask the line 29 question whenever any taxable pension, annuity or IRA income exists, and let the filer give the date they turned 59½.

findings.who: A filer under 59½ (born after mid-1966) who received taxable distributions as the beneficiary of a deceased parent's IRA or pension, where the decedent would have qualified for the exclusion.
findings.why_no: The gate checks only the recipient's own birth year, so no recipient is counted. The beneficiary clause exists only inside the gated question, and that question is reached only through this gate. In addition, the line's 'Otherwise: false, and the question below is not asked' means that when the gate is false the question is never asked at all. The beneficiary branch is unreachable.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 9, Line 29: 'If you received pension and annuity income and are married, or received pension and annuity income as a beneficiary, see Married taxpayers or Beneficiaries below.'
findings.fix: Make the gate 'any person had taxable pension, annuity or IRA income' (count > 0), with no age filter. Then ask whether the recipient turned 59½ by December 31, 2025, or received the money as the beneficiary of someone who died.

findings.who: Any filer whose gate evaluates false, that is, every young or beneficiary recipient of private pension or IRA income.
findings.why_no: The line's logic is self-defeating. When the gate holds, the choice resolves to 'No' because a recipient was born in 1965 or earlier. When the gate fails, the line is forced to false and the question is not asked. No path ever asks the question or yields yes.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 9, Line 29: 'Did you enter an amount of pension income or annuity income, or both ... that was not from a New York State or local government pension plan or federal government pension plan?'
findings.fix: Invert the gate so the question is asked when no recipient is known to be 59½. Alternatively, drop the gate and ask whenever taxable pension, annuity or IRA income exists, since the tool must refuse or compute in either case.

findings.who: A filer 59½ or older whose only qualifying income is periodic distributions from a government 457 plan, a 403(b) or a 401(k), which they do not think of as 'pension or IRA money'.
findings.why_no: The question says 'that pension or IRA money', and the help mentions only 'such income'. A filer with a 401(k) or 457 plan may read this as excluding their plan.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 9, Line 29: qualifying income includes 'periodic distributions from government (IRC § 457) deferred compensation plans' and 'a qualified cash or deferred profit-sharing or stock bonus plan [IRC § 401(k)]'.
findings.fix: Name the plan types in the question: 'pension, annuity, IRA, 401(k), 403(b), Keogh, or government 457 plan distributions'.

p. 9, Line 29, "If Yes, and you were 59½ before January 1, 2025, enter the qualifying pension and annuity income included in your 2025 federal adjusted gross income, but not more than $20,000."

findings.who: A married couple filing jointly. The spouse is a NYC teacher in the NYC Teachers' Retirement System, and the W-2 shows 414(h) in box 14. The primary filer, who answers the screening questions, works in the private sector.
findings.why_no: The gate helper is labelled only 'A government job in New York' or 'A public employer in New York'. It does not say 'you or your spouse', so the filer answers about their own job and says no. The spouse wording appears only in the gated line's helper, which is never reached.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 8, Line 21: 'Are you a public employee of New York State or its local governments? ... If Yes, enter the amount of 414(h) retirement contributions, if shown on any federal Form W-2'
findings.fix: Word the gate as 'Did you or your spouse work for New York State or a New York local government, school district, public authority, or public university at any time in 2025?'

findings.who: A state employee in the NYS Employees' Retirement System who retired or moved to a private employer in mid-2025. The 2025 W-2 from the state shows 414(h) contributions for the months worked.
findings.why_no: 'A government job' and the instruction's present-tense 'Are you a public employee' read as current status at filing time. The filer no longer has the job and answers no.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 8, Line 21: 'enter the amount of 414(h) retirement contributions, if shown on any federal Form W-2'
findings.fix: Ask about any time in 2025, or key the gate to any 2025 W-2 from a New York public employer.

findings.who: A MABSTOA bus operator, or an employee of a public authority or public benefit corporation that participates in NYSLRS (Thruway Authority, a BOCES, a public library, a community college). The W-2 shows 414(h) contributions.
findings.why_no: The filer does not think of a transit authority, school district or public corporation as 'a government job' or 'New York State or its local governments'. They answer no, and the list of retirement systems that would correct them is only in the gated question's help.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 8, Line 21: '– a member of the Manhattan and Bronx Surface Transit Operating Authority (MABSTOA) Pension Plan'; '– a member of the New York State and Local Retirement Systems'
findings.fix: List the retirement systems in the gate itself, or ask the gate as 'Does any 2025 W-2 for you or your spouse show 414(h) in box 14, or are either of you a member of any of these systems: ...?'

findings.who: A public school teacher in the NYS Teachers' Retirement System, or a SUNY or CUNY faculty member in the Optional Retirement Program, who thinks of the employer as a school or university rather than 'government'.
findings.why_no: The wording 'government job' and 'public employer' suggests agency or civil-service work, not teaching or university employment.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 8, Line 21: '– a member of the New York State Teachers' Retirement System; – an employee of the State or City University of New York who belongs to the Optional Retirement Program'
findings.fix: Name public schools, school districts, SUNY and CUNY in the gate wording or its help.
